papers.title: Sleep Homeostasis Has Circaseptan and Circatrigintan Cycles Over Year-Long Timescales.
papers.abstract: Sleep homeostasis, the process by which sleep pressure accumulated during wakefulness is dissipated across non-rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, can be quantified as the nightly rate of decline in slow-wave activity (SWA; 0.5-4 Hz). Disruption of this homeostatic process has been documented in a range of neurological disorders including epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease and REM sleep behaviour disorder, yet its long-term dynamics in healthy individuals remain uncharacterized. The advent of subscalp EEG (sqEEG) platforms now makes continuous, naturalistic sleep recording feasible over months, enabling longitudinal study of sleep homeostasis at an unprecedented scale. Here we report the first such characterization in 20 healthy adults recorded continuously over 12-15 months. SWA slope was predominantly negative across all subjects, confirming intact homeostatic regulation and was stable across sex and age. Continuous wavelet transform analysis revealed significant circaseptan (~7-day) and circatrigintan (~28-day) rhythmicity in the majority of subjects, independent of sex. These findings establish a normative baseline for long-term sleep homeostatic dynamics and suggest that homeostatic sleep pressure dissipation is organized across multiple timescales beyond the single night, with direct relevance for neurological conditions in which this process is disrupted.

papers.title: NeuralFieldManifold: Uncovering the Manifold Geometry of Local Field Potentials
papers.abstract: Manifold geometry has become a powerful framework for understanding how the brain organizes high-dimensional neural activity into compact, interpretable structure. To date, however, most theoretical and methodological advances in neural manifold analysis have focused on spiking activity, leaving unresolved a fundamental question: What are the geometric principles governing the dynamics of local field potentials (LFPs); population level signals reflecting integrated subthreshold and suprathreshold neural activity that are broadly integral to clinical and brain-computer interface settings. Here, we establish, analytically and empirically, that the lag-embedded dynamics of LFP signals lie on a low-dimensional K-torus, where K directly relates to sustained oscillatory modes present in the signal. Modeling LFPs as bounded autoregressive processes, we show that each oscillatory component contributes an independent circular degree of freedom, while aperiodic 1/f structure and noise contribute only geometric thickness around the manifold without altering its topology. To apply this theory to real nonstationary recordings, we introduce DeepLagField, a physics-informed network that jointly estimates time-varying AR structure and effective model order, with formal guarantees that local toroidal geometry is preserved despite non-stationary nature of neuronal processes. Persistent homology analysis on real recordings reveals topological signatures consistent with the predicted toroidal Betti numbers in primate V1 LFP, rodent hippocampal LFP, and mouse cortical EEG, with varying degrees of agreement across recordings and temporal windows. Crucially, decoding analyses across three distinct neural datasets demonstrate that these geometric structures are not merely descriptive but capture behaviorally relevant information rivaling conventional spectral features. Together, these findings establish a theoretically grounded and empirically validated geometric framework for neural field analysis, extending the manifold perspective beyond spiking activity and offering a complementary language to spectral analysis for understanding and translating population dynamics across neural modalities.

papers.title: Enhancing deep sleep with auditory stimulation to boost cognitive training responsiveness in people with Parkinson's disease and mild cognitive impairment: Rationale and design of the double-blind randomized controlled trial PD-CogT-Sleep
papers.abstract: Background: Cognitive training (CogT) is an established non-pharmacological intervention for people with Parkinson's disease (PD) and mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI). However, overall effects on cognitive outcomes are small to moderate and interindividually highly heterogeneous. Sleep -especially deep sleep- could be an important determinant of CogT responsiveness in PD, and may have beneficial effects on PD pathophysiology. Therefore, the enhancement of deep sleep by phase-targeted auditory stimulation (PTAS) could strengthen the effects of CogT on cognitive symptoms and counteract disease progression. Methods: PD-CogT-Sleep is a monocentric, partly decentralized, double-blind, randomized sham-controlled trial that combines two remotely delivered non-pharmacological interventions, to assess the additive effect of PTAS on digital CogT responsiveness in people with PD-MCI. The primary outcome is executive functions; Secondary and exploratory outcomes include further cognitive functions, participant-reported outcome measures, blood-based biomarkers, and high-density sleep electroencephalography markers. Outcomes are assessed at baseline, five weeks post-allocation and at 3-month follow-up. We aim to consecutively recruit N=50 participants, who will be randomized 1:1 to receive CogT+PTAS or CogT+Sham. Discussion: The PD-CogT-Sleep study integrates wearable and digital technologies to systematically combine a novel, non-invasive, sleep-enhancing intervention (PTAS) with established CogT to improve cognition and evaluate PTAS' disease-modifying potential through its effects on blood-based biomarkers in PD-MCI. The expected results will foster our understanding of the interplay of sleep, cognition, and neurodegeneration, and may guide further development of safe, feasible, scalable, patient-centered, technology-based non-pharmacological interventions counteracting cognitive decline in neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Beyond Classification Accuracy: Building Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence for Clinical Electroencephalography.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) remains important in clinical neuroscience because it records brain activity as a time-resolved physiological process. It offers millisecond temporal resolution, can be used at the bedside and supports prolonged monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded EEG analysis through automated pattern recognition, representation learning, large-scale screening and decision support in epilepsy, sleep medicine, cognitive disorders, psychiatric conditions, intensive care, disorders of consciousness and anaesthesia monitoring. High classification accuracy in a research dataset, however, is not clinical readiness. EEG signals are shaped by physiological state, artefacts, acquisition systems, preprocessing choices and clinical context. Labels may come from expert annotations, diagnostic categories, behavioural scales, treatment responses or long-term outcomes, and these sources do not always define the same biological target. This review argues that EEG-AI translation should be judged by the strength of its evidence, not by technical performance alone. We examine why EEG is valuable yet hard to standardize, how EEG features can serve as candidate biomarkers, and why translational maturity differs across clinical scenarios. We then discuss the evidence gaps behind high-performing models, focusing on target validity, data leakage, confounding, external validation and clinically aligned metrics. Finally, we argue for clinical understandability rather than model interpretability alone, and for human-machine workflows rather than isolated classifiers. Future EEG-AI systems should be assessed by whether their outputs are biologically plausible, externally generalizable, understandable to clinicians and safe in real-world care.

ai.summary: Reviews the translational evidence for AI-based clinical EEG analysis, arguing that high classification accuracy in research datasets does not establish clinical readiness and that translation should be judged by evidence strength rather than technical performance alone. The review examines target validity, data leakage, confounding, external validation, and clinically aligned metrics, and argues for clinical understandability and human-machine workflows over isolated classifiers.

papers.title: Electroencephalographic activity patterns distinguish interdigitated default and frontoparietal networks
papers.abstract: The brain is comprised of distributed functional networks that operate on diverse time scales. Evidence from precision fMRI shows that canonical networks, including default (DN), frontoparietal control (FPCN), and dorsal attention (dATN), each fractionate into multiple finely interdigitated networks. However, as fMRI is blind to fast processes underlying neural communication, there remains a need to neurophysiologically characterize individual-level network fractionation. To address this need, we conducted a simultaneous EEG-fMRI study, including multiple sessions per individual, resting-state and task conditions, and carbon wire loop sensors for optimized artifact correction. Using precision network mapping, we discovered dissociable electrophysiological correlates of blood-oxygen-level-dependent activity for two networks within the boundaries of the canonical DN. One (DNa) related more positively with alpha and high-beta power, while another (DNb) related more negatively with theta and low-beta power. Univariate and machine learning analyses further revealed electrophysiological dissociations between networks within the canonical FPCN (FPCNa versus FPCNb) but not dATN. The network-specific electrophysiological activity patterns were reliable across sessions, only modestly variable between resting-state and demanding task conditions, and observable for neighboring nodes of different networks across multiple cortical zones. Our findings provide insight into rhythmic neural processes that fine-grained networks may engage to support divergent cognitive operations.

Univariate and machine learning analyses also revealed electrophysiological dissociations between subnetworks of the frontoparietal control network but not the dorsal attention network, with patterns reliable across sessions.

papers.title: Clinical Validation of the New EEG Trend, Brain State of the Newborn, Against aEEG Interpretation.
papers.abstract: Previous studies have shown that the novel EEG trend, Brain State of the Newborn (BSN), is useful for monitoring recovery of electrocortical activity in high-risk newborns. Here, we validate the automatically computed BSN trend against visual amplitude-integrated EEG (aEEG) interpretation in asphyxiated hypothermia-treated infants. A total of 731 3-h aEEG epochs from 85 hypothermia-treated infants were randomized in order and scored independently by two clinical experts blinded for clinical data. First, we compared the BSN values to the aEEG scores at epoch level. Second, we assessed how the BSN trends align with aEEG scores in depicting electrocortical recovery. The BSN values showed robust differentiation between the experts' aEEG background scores (p ≤ 0.001 for all pairwise comparisons; effect size 1.0-6.5). Recovery of the BSN trend was also strongly correlated to the expert-defined aEEG recovery to continuous normal voltage (Spearman's ρ = 0.72, p < 0.001). The objective and fully automated BSN trend provides an effective, real-time complement to the visual aEEG interpretation. High BSN levels are reliable indicators of electrocortical recovery in hypothermia-treated infants. Future prospective studies are needed to establish evidence-based and context-sensitive clinical guidelines for the use of BSN in routine clinical care.

Concludes BSN offers a real-time automated complement to aEEG for assessing electrocortical recovery.

papers.title: Transient Alerting Effects of Karolinska Sleepiness Scale Ratings on Physiological and Driving Performance Indicators.
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to determine whether subjectively rating sleepiness on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS) gives rise to an alerting effect and, if so, how long it persists. Data from five driving simulator studies involving 83 participants were pooled. Time-locked trajectories of blink duration, blink closing velocity, heart rate, electroencephalographic (EEG) parietal α and frontal θ power, and lateral lane position variability were analysed around each KSS rating using linear mixed-effects models with condition-specific KSS baselines, a transient post-rating component, a late post-rating offset, and time-on-task terms. Immediately after the rating, several indicators shifted in an alerting direction: blink duration and standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP) decreased, blink closing velocity and heart rate increased, and parietal α power generally decreased. Frontal θ showed a more condition-dependent response. The estimated duration of the transient component was indicator dependent, ranging from 40 s for heart rate to the upper bound of the 120-s analysis window for SDLP. These findings have practical implications for driver sleepiness detection system development, validation protocols, and type-approval processes that rely on KSS as a reference measure. If ratings themselves are associated with short-lived physiological or behavioural changes, the timing and modality of KSS administration become important for ensuring valid ground truth labels. Future studies with control conditions, randomized or jittered rating times, and real-road data are needed to determine whether the rating-associated changes are causal and generalisable.

papers.title: Autonomic Reactivity and EEG-defined Clusters Reveal Distinct Chronic Pain Profiles.
papers.abstract: This study examined whether integrating stress-related heart rate variability (HRV) with resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) could characterize physiological subgroups in Chronic pain after spine surgery (CPSS). A total of 177 patients completed pain- and emotion-related questionnaires, a 3-minute resting-state EEG recording, and HRV assessments during baseline, mental arithmetic stress, and recovery. Participants were grouped by the direction of stress-related low-frequency/high-frequency (LF/HF) ratio change. Principal component analysis and unsupervised clustering were applied to 437 EEG features encompassing absolute power, cerebral asymmetry, and theta/beta ratio (TBR). After multivariate outlier detection, 168 participants underwent clustering. A 2 × 2 factorial ANOVA examined HRV-group and EEG-cluster effects on pain scores. LF/HF -decreased group (n = 56) reported higher depressive symptom scores than the increase group (n = 121, P = 0.045), without significant pain differences. Among 437 EEG features, PC1 reflected beta activity (34.39% variance), PC2 frontal/frontotemporal asymmetry (14.52%), and PC3 TBR features (9.55%). Two EEG clusters (n = 88 and n = 80) showed no significant pain- or emotion-related differences. Factorial analysis revealed nonsignificant HRV (P = .056) and EEG main effects (P = .107), but a nominally significant interaction [P = .030, partial η² = .028 (HC3-robust P = .044)]. Within EEG Cluster 0, the LF/HF-decrease group reported higher pain scores than the LF/HF-increase group (70.9 vs. 42.3; Tukey-adjusted P = .019). Integrating HRV-EEG profiles may help characterize CPSS heterogeneity. These exploratory findings, without study-wide multiplicity adjustment, require independent validation before clinical application.

ai.summary: In 177 patients with chronic pain after spine surgery, the authors integrated stress-related HRV LF/HF changes with resting-state EEG features via PCA and unsupervised clustering. A nominally significant HRV-group by EEG-cluster interaction was found, with the LF/HF-decrease group reporting higher pain scores within one EEG cluster, though main effects were not significant and findings require validation.

papers.title: Exchange of High-Frequency Medical Monitoring Data Using Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources for Interoperable Integration Into Clinical Practice and Research: Methodological Development Study.
papers.abstract: Continuous patient monitoring generates vast volumes of high-frequency monitoring data, such as electrocardiogram, electroencephalography, and invasive blood pressure tracings, that are often persisted in heterogeneous, noninteroperable formats, limiting integration with electronic health records and secondary use. Although Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) supports general health data exchange, native support for high-frequency medical monitoring data, including associated metadata and data quality metrics, remains limited. This study aims to develop a modality-agnostic FHIR package implementing a Metadata-Proxy pattern to enable scalable, semantically precise representation of high-frequency medical monitoring data, decoupling structured clinical metadata from raw signal storage. This study provides the FHIR package Time Series Integration and Data in Endpoints (TIDE), a collection of FHIR Release 4 artifacts for interoperable exchange and the standardization of high-frequency monitoring clinical data, using electroencephalography as the primary use case while remaining applicable to generic medical monitoring data. The core TIDE Observation profile separates technical metadata and analytical summaries stored directly in FHIR from high-volume raw data referenced via Endpoint resources. Quantitative results are standardized with pattern slicing, including sampling frequency, statistical summaries, and data quality metrics. Semantic interoperability was achieved through a hybrid terminology binding, using Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms, Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes for modalities, and custom CodeSystems for technical metadata, waveform modalities, channel identifiers, and connection types not covered by standard terminologies. All profiles were authored in FHIR Shorthand and compiled with SUSHI to produce a validated Implementation Guide conformant with the FHIR Release 4 core specification. The resulting framework provides a modality-agnostic structure for high-frequency monitoring data, comprising 7 primary FHIR artifacts that define 16 distinct component slices for metadata and signal analysis results. Observation resources reference associated Device and Endpoint instances, encapsulate acquisition parameters, and link to full-time-series repositories. Controlled vocabularies ensure unambiguous exchange, thereby enabling downstream use in research and decision support. The architecture decouples the metadata layer from the storage layer via a standardized Endpoint extension, enabling efficient querying of signals without retrieving large amounts of raw high-frequency monitoring data. TIDE provides a reusable, standards-compliant framework for integrating continuous high-frequency monitoring data into FHIR-based ecosystems. By separating semantically rich, queryable metadata from raw signal storage, TIDE enables longitudinal patient monitoring and automated signal quality-based triage without requiring modification of existing signal storage infrastructure.

papers.title: ST-M2EDA: spatio-temporal metric-guided multi-stream expert domain adaptation network for fatigue monitoring.
papers.abstract: In the human-machine collaboration paradigms of Industry 5.0, the intrinsic non-stationarity and domain drift of electroencephalogram (EEG) signals pose significant challenges to fatigue monitoring. Consequently, achieving accurate and robust cross-subject fatigue detection is paramount for workplace safety. This paper proposes a Spatio-Temporal Metric-Guided Multi-Stream Expert Domain Adaptation Network (ST-M 2 EDA). The framework initially employs Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)-based signal reconstruction to attenuate non-stationary noise, followed by Mixup data augmentation to enhance and smooth the feature space distribution. Furthermore, a hybrid architecture integrating Domain-Specific Batch Normalization (DSBN) with a ResNet-Transformer backbone is constructed to precisely decouple statistical discrepancies between domains. Finally, Multi-Kernel Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MK-MMD) is introduced as a dynamic routing criterion to facilitate fine-grained, adaptive decision-making for target samples. Experimental results on the SEED-VIG dataset demonstrate an average accuracy of 90.54%. Visual analysis of brain topography confirms that the model successfully aligns distributional shifts caused by individual heterogeneity-specifically correcting for specific frontotemporal lobe activation observed in subject S7-and establishes distinct decision boundaries. These findings indicate that synergizing signal reconstruction with Spatio-Temporal metric-guided multi-stream experts effectively mitigates negative transfer, ensuring reliable fatigue detection in complex cross-subject tasks.

papers.title: State-Dependent EEG Markers of Excitation/Inhibition and Hemodynamic State Are Associated with Random Noise Stimulation Effects.
papers.abstract: Non-invasive brain stimulation effects vary substantially across individuals, yet the physiological factors associated with this variability remain unclear. We tested whether baseline and task-related EEG markers of excitation/inhibition (E/I) and hemodynamic state are associated with the effects of transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) on learning. Participants completed a mathematical learning task during active or sham tRNS. We indexed E/I-related population dynamics using the EEG aperiodic exponent, for which lower values have been linked to relatively greater excitation than inhibition, and assessed hemodynamic state using fNIRS-derived oxygenated hemoglobin (HbO). Behavioral learning was modeled using generalized linear mixed-effects models. tRNS accelerated learning relative to sham stimulation but did not reliably induce pre-post changes in resting-state aperiodic exponent or HbO. Instead, stimulation effects were state-dependent. Higher resting-state aperiodic exponent and lower resting-state HbO were associated with greater behavioral gains under tRNS, while task-related aperiodic exponent was associated with stimulation-related differences in learning. Task-evoked HbO was associated with learning rate but did not significantly differentiate stimulation effects. Across modalities, the findings identify complementary electrophysiological and hemodynamic correlates of variability in learning under stimulation. However, statistical support for the EEG moderation effects was attenuated in models including participant-specific learning slopes, indicating sensitivity to random-effects specification and the need for replication. The findings argue against a simple tonic-shift account of tRNS and support a state-dependent framework in which stimulation effects depend on ongoing electrophysiological and hemodynamic context. EEG and fNIRS provided complementary information about variability in learning and stimulation response, supporting multimodal approaches to understanding and individualizing neuromodulation.

papers.title: LaBraM at Scale: Scaling Data and Models for EEG Pretraining
papers.abstract: LaBraM, an early EEG foundation model, demonstrated that large-scale EEG pretraining can yield strong representations for diverse downstream tasks. Building on this foundation, we expand pretraining data and model capacity while retaining its core encoder and objective. We train ten encoders with 5.8 million to 1.97 billion parameters on three EEG collections spanning 25,067 to 79,910 hours, adapting signal preparation and training to heterogeneous recordings. Across 23 tasks, Atom-L* reaches 59.05% mean balanced accuracy at its best evaluated full fine-tuning (Full-FT) checkpoint, 3.61 percentage points above the strongest baseline EEG foundation model. Quark-G leads linear probing (LP) at 54.33%, a 1.24-point margin. Both also lead average task rank. At the last evaluated checkpoints, larger encoders improve Full-FT more consistently than LP, and stronger LP does not guarantee stronger Full-FT. Preserving patch structure improves LP over average pooling. Data-fraction experiments suggest capacity-dependent saturation, while checkpoint trajectories show that downstream performance can decline as pretraining loss falls. Joint classification with a shared Qwen3 readout reaches 50.50% with Molecule-H and Qwen3-8B; increasing language-model size provides no consistent gain. These results demonstrate the value of scaling LaBraM and the importance of matching pretraining scale to downstream adaptation.

The largest model (Atom-L*) reached 59.05% mean balanced accuracy in full fine-tuning, 3.61 points above the strongest baseline EEG foundation model, and found that stronger linear probing did not guarantee stronger full fine-tuning.

papers.title: A Retrospective Real-World Assessment of Motor Status After Stroke Using a Home-Based Brain-Computer Interface
papers.abstract: Background: Upper extremity impairment persists in many stroke survivors, and few treatments are effective for severe chronic deficits. Brain-computer interface (BCI) therapy, which pairs decoded motor-intention-associated electrophysiology with sensory feedback, has improved upper extremity impairment in randomized trials, including in patients with severe paresis. Whether these benefits translate to routine care has rarely been evaluated. This study examined upper extremity motor recovery through 1 year among patients prescribed at-home BCI therapy in clinical practice. Methods: This retrospective observational study included adults who were prescribed the IpsiHand System, an electroencephalography-based BCI, through a commercial US home therapy program, had a baseline Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer (UEFM) assessment, and averaged >1 session per week through their last assessment. Occupational therapists administered the UEFM by video every 4 weeks. The primary outcome was UEFM change from baseline to week 12. A mixed model for repeated measures estimated change through week 52, with multiple imputation sensitivity analyses for missing data. Results: Of 452 patients included in analyses (mean time since stroke, 5.4 +/- 5.4 years), mean baseline UEFM was 20.1 +/- 14.6, with 333 patients (73.7%) having severe motor impairment (UEFM 0-28). At week 12, mean UEFM change was 4.3 points (95% CI, 3.7-4.9; P<0.001), and 31.7% achieved the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 5.25 points. Mean change reached the MCID at week 16 (5.6, 95% CI [4.8, 6.4]). Model-estimated change in UEFM continued to improve through 1 year, being 6.1 (95% CI, 5.5-6.8) at week 24 and 8.1 (95% CI, 6.8-9.4) at week 52. Conclusions: Among regular users of at-home BCI therapy in routine care, most of whom had severe chronic impairment, UEFM scores improved by 12 weeks, reached MCID by 16 weeks, and continued to increase through 1 year. At-home BCI therapy merits evaluation in randomized trials with follow-up beyond 12 weeks.

papers.title: GraTED: Graph--Tensor EEG Decoding for Passenger Hazard Perception in Autonomous Vehicles
papers.abstract: Passenger electroencephalography (EEG) can reveal road risk through anticipatory responses before hazardous events and neural reactions around their onset. However, existing EEG decoding methods often map physiologically meaningful arrangement of electrodes onto artificial 2D grids and thus flatten the higher-order time-feature representations into matrices, obscuring meaningful structure in the data. To preserve and exploit the spatial and time-feature structure of EEG recordings, we propose the Graph-Tensor EEG Decoding Model (GraTED) for passenger risk prediction (RP) and danger identification (DI) in autonomous-vehicle scenarios. GraTED models the electrode arrangement as an undirected graph based on their scalp locations, using graph convolution to capture spatial dependencies and low-rank tensor classification to preserve the multidimensional time-feature structure, while controlling model complexity. Evaluated on the PassengerEEG dataset, comprising 11 participants and 45 hours of recordings, GraTED achieves the highest balanced accuracy, compared to the state-of-the-art, across all three evaluation settings, while requiring the fewest learnable parameters among seven baseline methods.

papers.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
papers.abstract: Benitez, B, Kwak, M, Succi, PJ, Mitchinson, CJ, Snell, ER, and Bergstrom, HC. Gotta go fast: Intended concentric effort produces divergent myoelectric spectral profiles during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine how intended concentric velocity, that is, the volitional effort applied to accelerate a load, influences the spectral characteristics of the surface electromyographic (sEMG) signal during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. Twenty recreationally active adults (10 men and 10 women) performed unilateral leg extensions to task failure at 70% 1 repetition maximum under 2 within-participant conditions as follows: maximal intended concentric velocity (Vmax) and 50% of individualized Vmax (50%Vmax). Bipolar sEMG from the vastus lateralis was decomposed into 10 frequency bands using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Band-specific spectral intensities were modeled with a lognormal generalized linear mixed-effects model, and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (ρc) was computed between condition-specific spectral profiles across pairwise time points. The mean propulsive concentric velocity and total repetitions to task failure were secondary outcomes. Significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. The 3-way interaction of condition × frequency × repetition was significant (χ2(3) = 23.98, p < 0.001). Across the set, Vmax redistributed spectral power bidirectionally, increasing the low bands while suppressing the high bands, whereas 50%Vmax increased across the entire spectrum without high-frequency suppression. Despite these divergent profiles, the conditions converged at task failure (ρc = 0.98), and the convergence was asymmetric. The fatigued 50%Vmax profile approximated the fresh Vmax profile (ρc = 0.97) rather than the reverse (ρc = 0.74), indicating that submaximal effort approached the maximal-effort state as fatigue accumulated. The mean propulsive concentric velocity also declined 3.6 times more steeply under Vmax despite similar repetitions. Intended concentric velocity appears to shape the spectral profile of muscle excitation under fixed loading.

papers.title: Medicating inhibitory control? Treatment with serotonergic antidepressants predicts stop-N200 amplitudes in major depressive disorder.
papers.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a prevalent chronic mental illness often treated by serotonergic pharmacotherapy and complicated by sex differences and comorbid anxiety disorders (COMs). Deficits in inhibitory control are a transdiagnostic feature of MDD and COM, though the presentation of these deficits may be impacted by competing cognitive demands, symptoms severity, sexes, and medication status. This project includes 233 participants from the Tulsa 1000 study who completed concurrent electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetic functional resonance imaging (MRI) during a stop signal task (SST). We examined how serotonergic antidepressants, biological sex, and comorbidity with an anxiety disorder uniquely relate to neural indices of inhibitory control for healthy controls (HCs), MDD, and COM using linear mixed effect models, type III ANOVAs, and optimal full propensity matching. N200, P300, and correct-related negativity (CRN) components were extracted and analyzed to index conflict monitoring, conflict resolution, and performance monitoring, respectively, in response to stop signals and their absence. Our results revealed that HCs exhibited larger stop-P300 amplitudes than MDD and COM (η2 = 0.068); females had smaller stop-N200 amplitudes than males (η2 = 0.027); MDD/COM participants taking a serotonergic antidepressant exhibited less negative N200 amplitudes than those who were not (LME, B = 1.95; η2 = 0.044; ATE, B = 2.47). Our findings suggest being treated with serotonergic antidepressants are associated with neural differences in the conflict monitoring of inhibitory control in pure and comorbid depression.

papers.title: A multimodal dataset of EEG, eye-tracking, and physiological signals during naturalistic smartphone interactions
papers.abstract: Smartphones have become pervasive tools for communication, information consumption, and digital interaction, yet the neurophysiological dynamics associated with naturalistic smartphone use remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we present a multimodal physiological dataset collected during ecologically valid smartphone interaction and a subsequent relaxation condition. Twenty-three participants engaged with their most frequently used smartphone application (primarily gaming or short form video) for ten minutes, followed by a five-minute passive viewing of a standardized nature video. Simultaneous recordings were obtained from electroencephalography (EEG; 64 channels), wearable eye-tracking, photoplethysmography (PPG), and galvanic skin response (GSR) sensors. Questionnaire-based assessments, including the smartphone addiction scale (SAS) and the mobile phone problematic use scale (MPPUS), are also collected to characterize individual differences in smartphone-related behavioral traits. All data streams are synchronized using transistor-transistor logic (TTL) trigger signals to ensure precise temporal alignment across modalities. The dataset is organized according to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) specification and is publicly available on OpenNeuro (Accession Number: ds007537). This dataset enables the investigation of neural, ocular, and autonomic responses during smartphone interaction and supports multimodal analysis of diverse smartphone behaviors while preserving ecological validity.

papers.title: Diagnostic value of extending outpatient EEG to record sleep - A retrospective study.
papers.abstract: Evidence for the utility of sleep electroencephalography (EEG) in the diagnosis of epilepsy is inconsistent, often necessitating repeat visits and sleep deprivation (SD), which increases patient and resource burden. In our setting in India, patients are often referred for EEG immediately following consultation (single visit) and EEG sessions are extended to allow for spontaneous sleep acquisition without prior SD. We aimed to evaluate the success rate of achieving sleep during these extended outpatient recordings and its incremental diagnostic yield for interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs). We retrospectively analyzed 1762 outpatient EEGs from patients (45% female) with suspected or known epilepsy. All patients underwent an extended routine EEG (~40-50 min), incorporating standard activation procedures and aiming to capture spontaneous sleep where possible. Successful sleep acquisition was defined as the attainment of at least NREM stage N2. IED detection rates were compared between wakefulness and sleep across different epilepsy types. Sleep was achieved in 70.5% of patients (median age, 28 years; IQR: 16-55; range, 0.3-90). The proportion attaining sleep increased with recording duration, from 36.7% at 20 min to 55.6% at 30 min and 66.7% at 50 min, with a median time to sleep onset of 20 min. Among 1199 patients with both awake and sleep states captured, wakefulness identified IEDs in 29% (n = 350), while sleep captured unique IEDs in an additional 12% (n = 141), increasing the total yield significantly. In a sub-analysis of confirmed epilepsy cases (n = 751), wakefulness showed IEDs in 42% (n = 315), with sleep adding another 16% (n = 123). The diagnostic yield of sleep recordings was significantly higher than that of wakefulness alone (OR: 1.31; 95% CI: 1.02-1.68; p = 0.043), particularly among adults with idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) (OR: 2.20; 95% CI: 1.30-3.73; p = 0.004) and children with self-limited epilepsy (OR: ∞; p = 0.031). Despite a busy outpatient setting, 70.5% of patients attained N2 sleep during an extended EEG recording without SD. Sleep capture increased progressively with recording duration, with the greatest incremental gain between 20 and 30 min, suggesting that a modest extension beyond 20 min substantially increases the likelihood of capturing sleep. Sleep recording increased IED detection over wakefulness alone, particularly in children, in adults with IGE, and in self-limited epilepsies. Whether this approach can substitute for a sleep-deprived EEG requires prospective, head-to-head evaluation.

papers.title: A phase-calibrated combined electrical-sensory neuromodulation platform for short-Term frontoparietal network modulation and cognitive fatigue resistance.
papers.abstract: Non-invasive multimodal neuromodulation is often limited by cross-modal temporal misalignment caused by modality-specific conduction delays. To address this challenge, we developed a microcontroller-based multiphysics stimulation platform integrating transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) with visual and auditory rhythmic inputs. A feedforward delaycompensation strategy using individualized ERP latencies (visual P1 and auditory N1) was implemented to reduce intermodal timing discrepancies.The system was evaluated in a randomized, sham-controlled crossover study with 15 participants providing complete EEG datasets. Compared with sensory-only stimulation, the phase-coordinated multiphysics condition increased resting-state frontoparietal theta power and enhanced functional connectivity (wPLI). During a subsequent high-load cognitive task, it was also associated with reduced accumulation of fatigue-related parietal alpha power.Exploratory analysis revealed a moderate association between parietal alpha stability and behavioral performance (r = 0.577, p = 0.024). These findings suggest that temporally coordinated cross-modal stimulation may support more stable large-scale neural dynamics and improved cognitive performance under sustained load, providing a technical framework for precision multimodal neuromodulation.

papers.title: Repeated prefrontal transcranial direct current stimulation improves behavioral regulation and modulates resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with problematic smartphone use: a randomized sham-controlled longitudinal study.
papers.abstract: Problematic smartphone use (PSU) has emerged as an increasingly prevalent digital behavioral addiction among young adults and is associated with impaired executive control, excessive craving, and altered large-scale brain network organization. Although transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has demonstrated therapeutic potential for addictive disorders, its neurophysiological mechanisms in PSU remain insufficiently understood. This study investigated whether repeated prefrontal tDCS improves behavioral outcomes and reorganizes resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. Eighty participants meeting validated criteria for PSU were randomly assigned to receive active (n = 40) or sham (n = 40) tDCS. Active stimulation (2.0 mA, 20 min/session, three sessions/week for 12 weeks) targeted the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Behavioral outcomes included objectively recorded smartphone use, Smartphone Addiction Scale-Short Version scores, ecological momentary assessment craving, and work and social functioning. Resting-state EEG was recorded under eyes-closed and eyes-open conditions before and after intervention. Canonical EEG microstate temporal characteristics were analyzed using mixed repeated-measures analysis with false discovery rate correction. Compared with sham stimulation, active tDCS significantly reduced objectively measured smartphone use, craving intensity, and functional impairment while improving behavioral regulation. Neurophysiologically, active stimulation selectively reorganized resting-state brain dynamics. During eyes-closed recording, microstate C occurrence decreased whereas microstate D occurrence increased significantly. During eyes-open recording, both the occurrence and coverage of microstate B increased following active stimulation. No significant changes were observed in global explained variance, suggesting that repeated tDCS primarily modified the temporal organization rather than the spatial configuration of resting-state brain activity. Repeated prefrontal tDCS produced concurrent behavioral improvement and selective reorganization of resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. These findings provide preliminary evidence that repeated prefrontal tDCS is associated with concurrent behavioral changes and alterations in resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in young adults with PSU. Further confirmatory studies are needed to determine the clinical and mechanistic significance of these neurophysiological changes.

papers.title: Development and validation of a multimodal data-based scale for predicting epilepsy surgery outcomes.
papers.abstract: Seizure outcomes after drug-resistant epilepsy surgery are hard to predict, and existing models lack rigorous validation. We developed and internally validated a multimodal scale predicting seizure freedom. Retrospectively, 157 of 816 screened patients with complete data and ≥ 1 year follow-up were analyzed (116 seizure-free [SF], 41 non-seizure-free [NSF]). Predictors came from clinical variables, MRI, FDG-PET, video-EEG, and MEG. From 56 variables, eight predictors were fixed by screening, clinical judgment, four machine-learning algorithms, and minimum-AIC logistic regression, then re-estimated in all 157 patients by Firth's bias-corrected logistic regression without repeat selection. Internal validation used 2000 bootstrap resamples. A cutoff maximizing 0.4 ×sensitivity + 0.6 ×specificity was selected once in the full cohort and applied unchanged to the ≥ 24 months subgroup. The model retained disease duration, age at surgery, four EEG patterns, temporal MRI lesion, and unilateral unifocal PET hypometabolism. Development-phase AUCs (0.864 training, 0.810 test) were descriptive. Firth re-estimation gave an apparent AUC of 0.771 and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.724 (Brier 0.156/0.176). At the 79.64-point cutoff, sensitivity was 61.2% and specificity 85.4%; all 95% confidence intervals included the null. Among 101 patients followed ≥ 24 months, the locked model gave AUC 0.770 (95% CI 0.664-0.865), Brier 0.158, sensitivity 53.9%, specificity 96.0%. Multimodal data integration yielded a fully specified, reproducible eight-variable scale with stable discrimination in longer-term follow-up, supporting exploratory use for preoperative risk stratification and counseling alongside presurgical evaluation. Prospective multicenter validation is the next step toward clinical implementation.

papers.title: Intraoperative electroencephalography burst suppression during endoscopic third ventriculostomy: Case report and implications for neuromonitoring.
papers.abstract: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) is a common treatment for obstructive hydrocephalus. Intraoperative hemodynamic disturbances are well recognized. Their concurrent association with cortical suppression on electroencephalography (EEG), particularly burst suppression, has rarely been reported, and intraoperative EEG is seldom used during ETV. A 28-year-old woman underwent ETV for obstructive hydrocephalus secondary to a tectal glioma. Shortly after endoscope insertion and ventricular irrigation, she developed two successive episodes of severe tachycardia and an acute hypertensive crisis, each coinciding with an abrupt bilateral fall in fronto-temporal electrocortical activity with burst suppression on two-channel processed EEG. Irrigation was stopped and the endoscope was withdrawn. Systemic hemodynamics normalized within 15 min, whereas the EEG required 55 min to recover. The patient recovered to near-baseline within 4 h. This report represents only the second published case coupling an acute intraoperative hemodynamic surge with bilateral EEG burst suppression during ETV. Processed intraoperative EEG may be an additional early sign of an acute disturbance of cerebral function. Its added value remains unproven, since a hemodynamic emergency already mandates cessation of irrigation and endoscope withdrawal. Prospective evaluation with finer temporal sampling and raw-EEG recording is warranted.

papers.title: Neural and behavioral signatures of live and video demonstrations in bimanual interpersonal coordination: An EEG and kinematic study.
papers.abstract: Neural oscillations in the mu (8-12 Hz) and high-beta (21-30 Hz) bands are established markers of interpersonal coordination. However, the influence of social context-live versus video modeling - on sensorimotor engagement during coordinated action remains poorly understood. This study investigated how model type and engagement mode (execution vs. observation) shape neural and behavioral responses during an interpersonal motor coordination task. Twenty right-handed females (25.47 ± 3.4 years) were randomly assigned to train with either a live or video model (n = 10 per group). The same model performed 30-s sequences of elbow flexion-extension. Participants observed and executed the task with both live and video models across three phases (pre-test, post-test, and retention). During practice following the pre-test, participants trained coordinately with the model for 30 min. EEG activity was recorded from C3, Cz, and C4 electrodes, and spectral power was analyzed in the mu (8-12 Hz) and high-beta (21-30 Hz) bands. Kinematic coordination was quantified using vector coding of coupling angles between the participant and the model during execution. Results indicated significant desynchronization in both mu and high-beta bands during execution trials. Compared with the video-model condition, live-model interaction produced stronger high-beta suppression and more stable kinematic coupling. Additionally, mu suppression during observation increased across practice phases from pre-test to post-test and retention. Social context shapes interpersonal synchronization; physical presence may enhance perception-action coupling and predictive motor coding underlying joint action.

papers.title: Neural correlates of perceptual biases in duration perception.
papers.abstract: How we perceive a current event depends not only on its immediate context, but also on how our internal expectations are shaped by prior experience. In time perception, these expectations manifest as systematic biases, namely sequential dependence, where the current percept is influenced by the previous stimulus, and central tendency, the overestimation of short durations and underestimation of long ones. Both perceptual biases, corresponding to individual beliefs about stimulus generation, can vary substantially between participants. However, the neural responses related to inter-individual differences in these biases remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate this question in a duration reproduction task. Our EEG results show that in the frontocentral region, the Contingent Negative Variation (CNV) while experiencing the current stimulus depends on the previous stimulus regardless of sequential dependence. In contrast, in the right parietal region, the slow potential was not influenced by previous duration but associated with inter-individual differences in sequential dependence. Stimulus-offset evoked P2 amplitude was associated with both central tendency and sequential dependence and P2 amplitude varied with previous stimulus duration depending on individual sequential dependence. A Bayesian model of time perception reproduced the observed neural dynamics of the frontocentral CNV and its dependence on previous stimulus duration, suggesting that individual internal time estimates and expectations of stimulus offset are reflected in EEG responses. Our results demonstrate that both forms of perceptual bias are reflected in neural activity while experiencing the ongoing stimulus, suggesting that neural processes related to perceptual biases directly affect the measurement of time.

papers.title: Unexplained neurological deterioration after acute brain injury: A structured intensive care framework for targeted continuous electroencephalogram.
papers.abstract: Neurological deterioration after acute brain injury is common in the intensive care unit, yet its cause may remain uncertain when repeat imaging is stable or does not fully explain the examination. Delayed recognition of occult structural, vascular, systemic, metabolic, medication-related, or electrographic mechanisms may postpone time-sensitive treatment. We aimed to provide a structured bedside framework and define the role of targeted continuous electroencephalography (cEEG). We performed a narrative synthesis of evidence and consensus recommendations across aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracerebral hemorrhage, ischemic stroke, traumatic brain injury, and acute subdural hematoma, emphasizing bedside examination, repeat neuroimaging, vascular reassessment, systemic physiology, medication effects, and critical care electroencephalogram (EEG). Deterioration should first be confirmed as a true change and classified as explained, unexplained, disproportionate, or fluctuating/episodic. Evaluation should proceed in parallel: Correct reversible systemic and metabolic derangements, review sedative and analgesic exposure, and reassess structural or vascular complications. cEEG is most informative when deterioration remains unexplained after stabilization, exceeds the apparent imaging burden, fluctuates, follows a clinical seizure, or presents as delayed awakening. It can identify electrographic seizures, status epilepticus, and rhythmic or periodic patterns; however, a nonexplanatory recording neither establishes neurological stability nor excludes nonelectrographic secondary injury. A structured intensive care framework may reduce premature diagnostic closure and support timely, selective cEEG. Continuous EEG should complement, not replace, repeated clinical examination, neuroimaging, vascular evaluation, and correction of systemic physiology.

papers.title: Thought-deciphering via hierarchical EEG-to-text alignment
papers.abstract: Communication is important for our well-being, but it can be impaired by disabilities, such as locked-in syndrome (LIS), cerebral palsy (CP), and dysarthria. Non-invasive brain-to-text brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer a promising solution by providing an alternative communication pathway for people with communication disabilities. However, most recent breakthroughs have relied on large, cumbersome, and costly neuroimaging modalities, such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). Numerous studies have attempted decoding using the lighter and cheaper electroencephalography (EEG), but the results remain inferior compared to the other modalities. More importantly, we do not understand how these modalities are related to text at the letter, word, sentence, and higher semantic levels. Many prior studies have focused on decoding below the sentence level because it is considerably easier to design an experiment around phonemes, letters, and words. However, during communication, sentences play a much more important role than words and letters. This is because sentences carry information at such a high level that they can be understood even if some words and letters are missing. However, within sentence-level decoding, sentence classification is not as well investigated as sentence generation, making it difficult to decide whether a sentence should be retrieved or generated in the context of EEG-to-text decoding. This paper strives to investigate sentence-level EEG-to-text classification via a novel hierarchical alignment framework, where the main goal is to retrieve a read sentence using its context and EEG as inputs.

papers.title: In-person UCLA-PEERS® program for adolescents with autism spectrum disorder in Italy: study protocol for a pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial with pragmatic features and exploratory EEG markers of treatment response.
papers.abstract: Adolescents with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Level 1 frequently experience persistent difficulties in peer relationships and social functioning that become more evident as social demands increase. Group-based social skills trainings represent a key evidence-based intervention for this population, yet its availability in routine clinical services is still limited. The Program for the Education and Enrichment of Relational Skills (PEERS®) is one of the most empirically supported interventions for autistic adolescents. In Italy, telemedicine delivery has shown promising results, but the effectiveness and implementation of the in-person format in real-world services have not yet been evaluated. In addition, predictors of individual response to psychosocial interventions remain largely unknown. This study is designed as a two-arm pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial incorporating pragmatic features, including delivery within a routine tertiary clinical service, comparison with Treatment as Usual (TAU), and allowance for ongoing concomitant clinical, educational, and pharmacological treatments. It will compare the in-person Italian adaptation of UCLA PEERS® with Treatment as Usual (TAU) at IRCCS Fondazione Stella Maris (Pisa, Italy). Thirty-six adolescents aged 11-13 years with ASD (DSM-5-TR) and Full-Scale IQ >85 will be assessed at baseline (T0) and after the 16-week intervention (T1). Randomization will use block allocation with allocation concealment until completion of baseline assessments; outcome assessors and independent ADOS-BOSCC video coders will remain blind to group assignment. The intervention includes sixteen weekly 90-minute group sessions delivered by certified providers, with parallel caregiver sessions and structured teacher contacts to promote generalization. The primary focus of this pilot trial is feasibility, assessed through recruitment, retention, session attendance, and treatment fidelity. Clinical outcomes will be examined exploratorily to provide preliminary estimates of treatment effects. The QSQ-R will serve as the prespecified principal clinical outcome for estimating change in social functioning from baseline to T1. Parent- and adolescent-report versions will be analyzed separately, considering the Social Initiative and Social Reciprocity dimensions as distinct outcomes rather than deriving a composite total score. Key secondary outcomes include social knowledge (TASSK-R), autism-related social responsiveness (SRS-2), social motivation (SSDS), social anxiety (SAS), and observational change in social-communication behaviors (ADOS-BOSCC). Emotional-behavioral functioning (CBCL; YSR) will be explored as additional secondary outcomes. Baseline electroencephalography (EEG) recorded during a gesture-word integration task will be used to derive the N400 congruency effect and to explore whether individual differences in this measure are associated with treatment response. As a pilot and feasibility trial, the study is not powered for definitive efficacy testing and will estimate feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, and preliminary effect sizes to inform future multicenter trials. This study will provide the first evaluation of in-person PEERS® in the Italian clinical context and test the generalizability of previous telemedicine findings in routine care. The integration of clinical and behavioral outcomes may contribute to mechanism-informed, personalized psychosocial interventions for autistic adolescents and guide the design of future confirmatory studies. (ClinicalTrials.gov - NCT07207213 - October, 3, 2025).

papers.title: Multimodal characterization of putative pan-inhibitory viral constructs in macaque monkeys
papers.abstract: Transgenic approaches and validated viral vector toolboxes have advanced our understanding of how inhibitory neurons shape cognition and motor control in mice and other rodents. However, such advances have been elusive in non-human primates (NHPs). While many studies demonstrate expression of reporter proteins, few studies have provided clear quantitative evidence of whether these viral constructs can be reliably used for assessment of in vivo and in vitro function in primates, which, in turn, has hindered widespread adoption by NHP researchers. Here, we characterize putative pan-inhibitory cell targeting vectors engineered with regions from the Dlx5-6 intergenic domain. Pan-inhibitory viral vectors are attractive because they enable ground-truth optotagging and modulation of multiple inhibitory subtypes in the same animal and, when combined with machine learning approaches, enable cell-type classifiers for NHPs. We combined in vivo anesthetized electrophysiological recordings, in vitro slice electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry across seven rhesus macaque monkeys to assess the specificity, completeness and efficacy of three constructs in multiple sensory and higher-order association cortices. The vectors reliably restricted transgene expression to inhibitory neurons (81-97%). However, of the local GABAergic neurons only 32-64% expressed the transgene, depending on the construct. This incompleteness arose in part from uneven coverage across subtypes, with strong transgene expression in parvalbumin-positive interneurons (~60-90%), sparse expression in calbindin-positive interneurons (~1-7%), and near-complete avoidance of calretinin-positive interneurons. A construct pairing DLX2.0 with ChrimsonR was excellent for in vivo optotagging, while h56D paired with bReaChES most effectively suppressed neural activity in vivo. In the slice, activating terminals of transgene-expressing neurons optically evoked inhibitory currents in coupled pyramidal neurons confirming transsynaptic functionality of these constructs and their use for inhibitory circuit-specific synaptic assessments and manipulation. Collectively, the results provide rigorous functional characterization, and quantitative guidance for NHP researchers seeking to deploy GABAergic cell-type-specific tools in their experiments.

papers.title: Machine learning-assisted chemometric analysis of salivary ATR-FTIR spectra for the diagnosis of oral submucous fibrosis.
papers.abstract: Oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF) is a chronic, potentially malignant disorder strongly linked to areca nut chewing. Clinical diagnosis is challenging, and histopathology, though the gold standard, is invasive and subject to inter-observer variability. Saliva analysis using Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy offers a promising non-invasive alternative. This study evaluated salivary ATR-FTIR spectral analysis integrated with machine learning for classification of OSMF, individuals with adverse oral habits, and healthy controls. Unstimulated saliva samples were collected from 450 participants comprising 150 patients with clinically diagnosed OSMF, 150 individuals with adverse oral habits without clinical evidence of OSMF, and 150 healthy controls. After centrifugation, the saliva supernatant was analyzed by ATR-FTIR spectroscopy over 400-4000 cm-¹. Spectra underwent baseline correction and normalization followed by Savitzky-Golay smoothing. For machine-learning analysis, Standard Scaler and PCA were incorporated within the classification pipeline. Decision Tree, Random Forest, support vector machine (SVM), and XGBoost classifiers were evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. Hyperparameter optimization and performance estimation used the same cross-validation framework. An independent cohort of 90 participants was used for validation. XGBoost showed the highest cross-validation performance, with accuracies of 90.62% for Normal versus Habit, 97.67% for Normal versus OSMF, and 91.30% for three-class classification. Statistical analysis identified 157 nominally significant wavenumbers (p<0.05) within a continuous region from 1581 to 2142 cm-¹ corresponding to protein and collagen bands. Principal component analysis showed that PC1 and PC2 explained 89.26% and 6.95% of the total variance, respectively (96.21% cumulatively). In the independent validation cohort, accuracy was 80.0% for OSMF versus Normal and 71.7% for Habit versus Normal. Salivary ATR-FTIR combined with machine learning demonstrated promising classification performance and preliminary performance in an independent cohort. The identified spectral region is biologically plausible in the context of altered salivary biochemical composition associated with inflammation and fibrosis, but it should not be regarded as a validated disease-specific biomarker. Salivary ATR-FTIR is best considered a complementary, non-invasive screening and risk-stratification approach rather than a replacement for clinical/oral examination or histopathological assessment when biopsy is indicated. Larger, diverse, multicenter studies with rigorous validation are needed before clinical implementation.

papers.title: Case Report: Successful treatment of drug-resistant epilepsy with unilateral deep brain stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus.
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation of the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT-DBS) is an established palliative treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) and is conventionally performed bilaterally. However, the efficacy of unilateral ANT-DBS remains unclear. We report a patient with DRE who underwent unilateral ANT-DBS because of an epileptogenic network predominantly involving one side and anatomical constraints precluding electrode implantation on the contralateral side. A 29-year-old female underwent comprehensive presurgical evaluation, including seizure semiology assessment, video-electroencephalography (EEG), computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging. She developed DRE following multimodal treatment for a suprasellar germ cell tumor during childhood. Despite multiple antiseizure medications and vagus nerve stimulation, she continued to experience approximately 10 habitual seizures per day. Seizure semiology was characterized by asymmetric tonic posturing of the limbs lasting 10-30 s, followed by an atonic phase. EEG findings indicated a widespread epileptogenic network predominantly involving the right frontal and temporal areas. Brain imaging showed severe left hemispheric atrophy, marked widening of the left subdural space, and a pre-existing shunt system, which prevented identification of the left ANT. Therefore, DBS implantation was performed in the right ANT alone. Stimulation was initiated 7 days after surgery at an intensity of 2 mA. Following initiation of right ANT stimulation, seizure frequency decreased from approximately 10 to one per day, likely due to a microlesioning effect. Thereafter, right ANT stimulation was associated with a sustained seizure reduction of approximately 60%. Postoperative EEG demonstrated a reduction in interictal epileptiform discharges. The clinical benefit was maintained at the 9-month follow-up, with no surgery- or stimulation-related adverse events were observed. Unilateral ANT-DBS can provide clinically meaningful seizure control in carefully selected patients whose predominant epileptogenic network is localized to one cerebral hemisphere. This approach may represent a feasible therapeutic option when anatomical or surgical constraints prevent conventional bilateral ANT electrode implantation. Further studies with larger patient cohorts and longer follow-up periods are required to clarify the indications, durability, and efficacy of unilateral ANT-DBS.

papers.title: An integrative view of human nociceptor diversity: from microneurography to molecular identity.
papers.abstract: Neuropathic pain arises from dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system and affects up to 10% of the population worldwide. Aberrant activity in injured sensory nerve fibers, particularly spontaneous firing and altered conduction properties of nociceptors, is tightly linked to pain, yet its molecular underpinnings in humans have long remained elusive. Over recent years, major technological advances have transformed both functional and molecular analyses of sensory neurons. High-resolution single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have produced detailed atlases of sensory neuron diversity, while traditional electrophysiological approaches such as patch-clamp and microneurography have provided unparalleled insight into nerve fiber properties. Despite their individual strengths, molecular and functional classifications of sensory neurons have largely evolved in parallel. This review focuses on emerging strategies that bridge these approaches to achieve an integrated, mechanistic understanding of neuropathic pain. We discuss how microneurography-defined biophysical hallmarks, such as activity-dependent slowing, recovery cycle signatures, and following frequency, can be transferred into in vitro patch-clamp paradigms, enabling direct functional comparison with dissociated human and large-animal sensory neurons. The incorporation of Patch-seq approaches has further enabled the assignment of molecular identity to functionally defined nociceptor subtypes, exemplified by the characterization of the mechano-insensitive "sleeping" nociceptors. Finally, we highlight how multimodal datasets combining electrophysiology, transcriptomics, and computational modeling provide new opportunities to unravel the ion channel mechanisms, particularly sodium channel subtypes, that shape pathological firing states. By directly linking human nerve fiber function to molecular programs, this integrative framework paves the way toward stratified, mechanism-based therapies for neuropathic pain.

papers.title: Mapping Brain-Computer Interface Research in Depression (1995-2026): A Bibliometric Analysis.
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as promising tools for neuromodulation and emotion regulation in depression. This study aimed to systematically map the global research landscape, thematic evolution, and emerging trends of BCI applications in depressive disorders through bibliometric analysis. Data were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and analyzed using the R package bibliometrix, VOSviewer, and CiteSpace. Publication trends, country and institutional contributions, journal impact, author influence, and keyword-based clustering and burst analysis were comprehensively evaluated. A total of 239 publications authored by 1284 researchers from 239 institutions across 39 countries were identified. The United States and China had the highest publication outputs, while the United Kingdom showed high citation impact. Laureate Institute for Brain Research was the most productive institution and showed the strongest institutional collaboration, while NeuroImage: Clinical showed the highest journal h-index. Masaya Misaki was the leading author according to publication and citation indicators. Keyword analysis identified six major thematic clusters involving neurophysiological and cognitive features, EEG asymmetry and affective regulation, clinical neurofeedback, connectivity and self-regulation, fMRI-based emotion regulation, and psychiatric symptom/network correlates. "Emotion" showed the strongest keyword burst, while recent bursts in "real-time fMRI neurofeedback," "prefrontal cortex," and "emotion regulation" indicated increasing research attention to circuit-level regulation. The field has evolved from EEG-based characterization toward network-level and real-time neurofeedback research. These findings identify emerging research directions while highlighting the need for further methodological standardization and clinical validation.

papers.title: Calcified choroid plexus papilloma of the temporal horn presenting with seizures in an adult without hydrocephalus: An illustrative case.
papers.abstract: Choroid plexus papillomas (CPPs) are rare, benign tumors that typically occur in pediatric patients and result in hydrocephalus. Presentations in an adult featuring seizures, particularly focal impaired awareness seizures, occur infrequently, especially in the absence of hydrocephalus. A 50-year-old female exhibited episodes of temporary unresponsiveness characteristic of a focal impaired awareness seizure. Imaging identified a calcified mesial temporal lesion; electroencephalogram revealed epileptiform discharges. Surgical pathology confirmed the presence of CPP. The patient began treatment with levetiracetam and later underwent surgical removal of the tumor. Postoperatively, the patient experienced no seizures and exhibited no neurological deficits. While CPPs usually cause hydrocephalus, this case had no ventricular enlargement on imaging. Instead, a calcified CPP diagnostically mimicked a cavernoma by presenting solely with seizures and a calcified intraventricular temporal-horn mass in a 50-year-old adult; typically, CPPs present in the fourth ventricle rather than the temporal horn, whereas cavernomas regularly present in the temporal lobe with a classically "popcorn-like" appearance. Thus, CPPs can cause focal seizures via local cortical irritation that is calcified, similarly to a cavernoma; CPPs can also present in a middle-aged adult rather than a pediatric patient and lack the most common diagnostic sign of hydrocephalus. The cumulative rarity of a CPP that lacks hydrocephalus, causes seizures, contains calcifications, and manifests later in life makes for an incredibly atypical and unique case of CPP. Without pathology, the given symptoms and imaging were more suggestive of a cavernous malformation rather than a CPP, highlighting the importance of biopsy for an accurate diagnosis; early surgical resection is crucial and may be curative.

papers.title: A multimodal optimisation framework for cardiac electrophysiology model personalisation using computed tomography and 12-lead electrocardiogram: Algorithm development and validation.
papers.abstract: Accurate parameterisation of cardiac patient-specific models is a major challenge. Here we aimed to test the feasibility of an optimised multimodal personalisation framework that combines structural information from computed tomography (CT) and 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) features, for high-fidelity simulations of ventricular tachycardia (VT). We studied a small cohort of six patients who had CT images and sinus-rhythm 12-lead ECGs available prior to VT ablation. The CT images were used to construct patient-specific biventricular simulation domains and to estimate ECG lead positions. We implemented a graphics processing unit-based computational pipeline and a two-stage optimisation framework consisting of: (i) an early activation onset estimation; and, (ii) the optimisation of conductivity parameter. For validation, the simulation outcomes were compared to clinical VT patterns and cycle lengths. Following early onset estimations, simulated 12-lead ECG signals achieved a 91.20 % mean Q wave, R wave, and S wave (QRS) peak accuracy. Using the optimised parameters, average QRS duration error was reduced to 3.94 ms, compared to 37.42 ms for baseline parameters. Notably, in four patients with available electro-anatomical VT maps, simulations reproduced the clinical VT patterns and cycle length closer to recordings than those obtained with baseline parameterisation. Our pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of a robust electrophysiology modelling framework able to perform multimodal personalisation by integrating sinus-rhythm ECGs and cardiac CT images for VT simulations with tractable computational time, paving the way for its clinical translation and a less invasive scar-related VT risk assessment.

papers.title: Atypical Pediatric Epilepsy: A Narrative Review of Classification, Diagnosis, and Emerging Therapeutics.
papers.abstract: Atypical pediatric epilepsies represent a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by uncommon etiologies, variable clinical presentations, and frequent resistance to standard antiseizure medications. Recent advances in classification, along with developments in genomics, neuroimaging, and autoimmune neurology, have expanded the recognized spectrum of these conditions. However, a significant proportion of children remain without a definitive syndromic diagnosis, underscoring ongoing limitations in current frameworks. This review provides a comprehensive overview of atypical epilepsy in children, including evolving classification systems, epidemiology, and etiological mechanisms spanning genetic, structural, metabolic, and immune-mediated causes. Key syndromes - including Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome, infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, and febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome - are discussed with emphasis on clinical features, differential diagnosis, and prognosis. Diagnostic challenges such as phenotypic overlap, EEG limitations, and barriers to timely genetic testing are also examined. Emerging therapeutic strategies highlight a paradigm shift from broad-spectrum seizure control toward precision medicine, including targeted pharmacologic agents, antisense oligonucleotides, gene therapies, and neuromodulation approaches. Improved recognition and classification of atypical epilepsies, coupled with early implementation of targeted therapies, are essential to optimize outcomes in this vulnerable population.

papers.title: Restitution properties during ventricular fibrillation and the effects of cardiac pacing location on ventricular electrophysiology in the rabbit heart.
papers.abstract: Sudden cardiac death is a cause of mortality due to malignant arrhythmias such as ventricular fibrillation (VF). Although action potential duration (APD) restitution is a method to assess arrhythmic susceptibility, repolarisation may depend on prior activation history, a phenomenon known as cardiac memory. Cardiac memory describes the persistence of repolarisation effects from previous beats, such that APD reflects not only the immediately preceding diastolic interval (DI) but also earlier activation effects. This may be relevant during VF, where continuously varying activation patterns prevent a steady electrophysiological state. This study investigated how pacing location affects ventricular electrophysiology and whether repolarisation during VF exhibits short-term cardiac memory. Langendorff-perfused rabbit hearts were used to record monophasic action potentials from the left ventricular apex and base. Pacing was conducted from five sites. Steady-state APD was assessed during constant pacing. Effective refractory period (ERP), APD restitution and conduction time restitution (CTR) were assessed using an S1-S2 extra-stimulus protocol (S1, conditioning stimuli; S2, premature extra-stimulus). Additionally, APD-DI and APD-APD relationships were analysed during early VF. Pacing location significantly influenced S1 and S2 conduction delays, consistent with site-dependent activation timing. However, steady-state APD, ERP and CTR were not significantly affected by pacing location. In contrast, during VF, APD exhibited a significant dependence on preceding DI and preceding APD over approximately the first 30 beats, with these relationships progressively deteriorating thereafter. These findings demonstrate that while pacing location alters activation timing, repolarisation dynamics under stable activation histories are robust. During VF, continuously changing activation patterns unmask short-term cardiac memory.

papers.title: Study on methods for deriving spatial distribution of electron temperature and density from RGB (red-green-blue) digital image in non-thermal equilibrium plasma.
papers.abstract: A method used to derive the spatial distributions of electron temperature and density in non-thermal equilibrium plasma, respectively, from the relative and absolute intensities of RGB (red-green-blue) JPEG (Joint Photographic Experts Group) images acquired by using a digital camera is investigated. Since the RGB values of the JPEG image obtained from the complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor sensor of commercial digital cameras are automatically corrected, the RGB values are calibrated by simultaneously observing lamps with known RGB values using the camera and a spectrometer calibrated for absolute sensitivity as well as determining the correlation between the RGB values and emissivity. The validity of the calibrated RGB values is confirmed by observing the blackbody radiation of a candle flame using the camera and the spectrometer. In the case of optically thin plasmas, excitation radiation with a stronger intensity than bremsstrahlung radiation is observed. Since this strong excitation radiation is reflected in the RGB values, the electron temperature is derived from the relative RGB values by relating the excitation temperature obtained by using the line-pair method to the electron temperature obtained from continuum spectral analysis using bremsstrahlung radiation. The average grayscale calculated from the RGB values reflects the density distribution of the object's presence. The spatial distributions of electron temperature and density are obtained from the digital image using RGB relative values and the average grayscale, respectively.
